embeddingRow.description: A row of index.jsonl. text_sha256 binds the vector to the exact text embedded, so a vector can be shown stale per chunk and not merely per set. raw_norm is the vector's length BEFORE normalization: it is recorded because a raw norm of zero means the model extracted no signal from that chunk, which normalization would otherwise hide behind a division.

description: The manifest of one embedding set: the vectors produced for a chunk build by exactly one named model. Vectors live in a sidecar rather than inside the chunk records, because a chunk is a deterministic function of the corpus alone while a vector is a function of the corpus AND a model -- binding them into one file would make a chunk set change every time a model did, and would forbid holding two models' vectors for the same corpus. This manifest is the binding between the two, and it is what makes a vector attributable: the model that produced it, what kind of similarity it supports, which chunk build it covers, and how much of that build it actually covers.

built_from.description: The chunk build these vectors cover. corpus_digest changes whenever any covered chunk changes, so a stale set is detectable without re-reading the corpus.

coverage.description: Partial coverage is legal; SILENT partial coverage is not. Whenever skipped is above zero, reason states why, so a consumer never has to infer that a missing chunk was deliberate.

deterministic.description: True when this model is contracted to produce bit-identical vectors for the same input on any host. Only a set that claims this is gated on byte-identity across two builds; a learned model on varying hardware honestly claims false and is checked on its invariants instead.

index.description: One embeddingRow per vector, in row order, mapping each row back to the chunk it came from.

model.description: The name of the model that produced every vector in this set. Never null: a set exists only because a named model produced it. For a third-party model this is its published identifier, so a consumer can obtain the same model.

normalize.description: l2 = every stored vector has unit length, so a dot product is a cosine. none = raw vectors, and a consumer must normalize before comparing.

parts.description: The chunk files this set was built from, each with the digest of its bytes. An incremental rebuild compares these to decide which parts it need not look at; the per-row text digest in index.jsonl decides which rows it may reuse. Optional: a set written before parts existed simply offers no coarse filter, and rebuilds in full.

quantized.description: The BCIR-native view of the same vectors: signed int16 in BCIR's symmetric Q15 code space, row-major, little-endian, in the same row order. It exists so corpus retrieval can run on `bcir_ai_q15_topk` -- the exact squared-L2 top-k kernel runtime/c already uses for BCIR's own optimization memory -- rather than on a second convention this corpus would have to defend alone. Exact integer distances also mean the ranking has no floating-point tie-break to disagree about across hosts. Null when `normalize` is `none`, because the projection assumes unit vectors: quantizing unquantifiable magnitudes would saturate rather than approximate.

row_squares.description: ||p||^2 for every row of the Q15 codes, in the same row order: a materialized derived column. Optional, and absent from every set built before it existed -- a reader that does not find it computes the same values from `path`, which is what it did for every set until now. It is stored because the computation is a pure function of bytes that are already on disk and costs 69.5 ms of the 243 ms a default ranked query takes, repeated in every process, to rebuild 8,860 bytes. The values are NOT constant: on this corpus 2,212 of 2,215 are distinct, spread 0.057% around scale^2, so the term cannot be dropped from the distance -- only stored. `derived_from` is the digest of the codes these squares were computed over, so a reader can tell 'the squares of these codes' from 'squares'.

derived_from.description: The sha256 of the Q15 codes these squares were derived from.

scale.description: Coordinate v maps to round(v * scale), clamped to [-scale, scale].

symmetric.description: Always true: -32768 is excluded so the code space stays symmetric about zero and negation is lossless, the same discipline runtime/c applies to Q8 (-128 forbidden) and Q4 (-8 forbidden).

revision.description: The pinned version of that model -- a weights revision for a published model, or the algorithm version for a built-in one. Two sets with the same model and different revisions are not comparable.

semantics.description: What kind of similarity these vectors support. `lexical` = a specified function of the surface text (n-grams, hashing, term counts); near-duplicate text scores high, a paraphrase does not. `learned` = trained weights that place related meanings near each other. Both are legitimate and both are named, but they are NOT interchangeable, and a set that does not declare which cannot have its retrieval quality assessed. This is the same discipline the performance chapters apply to measured/modelled/estimated.

vectors.description: Raw little-endian float32, row-major, `dim` floats per row, row order given by index.jsonl. A flat binary rather than JSON floats: it is what a vector index ingests, it is an order of magnitude smaller than the decimal spelling, and it is byte-comparable, which is what makes the determinism check exact.
